evidence.claim: AEP Ohio states that the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio adopted its 2024 Data Center Tariff settlement on July 9, 2025 and that new data centers or expansions seeking service must apply through its process.
AEP Ohio reported that, as of February 12, 2026, data centers or developers had signed binding contracts for 5,642 MW, while earlier requests had exceeded 30,000 MW.
evidence.source_title: AEP Ohio Updates PUCO on Data Center Load: Figures Show Tariff is Working

evidence.claim: AEP Ohio's tariff approval included increased minimum billing demand charges for data-center customers and followed a moratorium linked to studying roughly 30,000 MW of anticipated data-center load.
evidence.source_title: Public Utilities Commission of Ohio Authorizes Tariff for AEP Ohio’s Data Center Customers

evidence.claim: A data-center tariff tracker reported that, as of March 31, 2026, 77 emerging large-load tariffs were pending or in place across 36 states.
evidence.source_title: JEPIC-USA - Large Load Tariffs Grow Prevalent as States Regulate Data Centers

evidence.claim: Virginia regulatory material indicates Dominion-related proceedings include data-center load growth reporting and alternative transmission cost allocation review, making cost allocation a live catalyst in the largest U.S. data-center market.
evidence.source_title: NARUC - April 13, 2026 large load and transmission cost allocation discussion

evidence.claim: Talen and Amazon's nuclear PPA/co-location structure is being treated as a major test case for data-center power procurement, while FERC has reviewed co-location issues in PJM.
evidence.source_title: POWER Magazine - Talen, Amazon Launch $18B Nuclear PPA

evidence.claim: GE Vernova's Q1 2026 materials state that its Electrification segment booked $2.4 billion of equipment orders to support data centers, more than all of the prior year, and that gas-power slot reservations increased.
evidence.source_title: GE Vernova Reports First Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Raises 2026 Guidance

evidence.claim: GE Vernova's Q1 2026 presentation lists switchgear, transformers, capacitors, HVDC systems, substations, and Prolec GE transformer expansion as relevant grid-modernization and data-center equipment exposures.
Eaton reported record Q1 2026 results and said the rolling twelve-month average of Electrical Americas orders rose 42%, driven by data-center momentum.
evidence.source_title: Eaton Reports Record First Quarter 2026 Results

evidence.claim: Eaton's Q1 2026 analyst presentation states that Electrical Americas data-center orders were up approximately 240% in Q1.
evidence.source_title: Eaton First Quarter 2026 Earnings Release / Analyst Presentation

evidence.claim: Quanta Services' Q1 2026 release identifies future opportunities in electrical grid modernization, upgrades, hardening, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and larger transmission infrastructure.
evidence.source_title: Quanta Services Reports First Quarter 2026 Results

evidence.claim: Vertiv is mapped to the high-density cooling and data-center power-distribution node because current industry reporting links AI infrastructure demand to Vertiv's liquid cooling, modular deployment, energy storage, and predictive maintenance offerings.
evidence.source_title: Data Center Frontier - Vertiv’s AI Infrastructure Surge

evidence.claim: Industry reporting in April 2026 said nearly half of planned U.S. data-center builds were delayed or canceled, with transformers, switchgear, and batteries cited as key electrical infrastructure constraints.

evidence.claim: A 2026 academic preprint argues that grid-supporting equipment supply chains constrain the feasible pace of power-system expansion, supporting the equipment-bottleneck thesis at the system level.

memory_update.text: New Hotspots should be tracked as an AI power-access chain: hyperscaler demand -> utility interconnection -> tariff/cost allocation -> transmission upgrades -> transformers/switchgear/substations -> EPC execution -> on-site power/cooling.
Highest bottleneck score belongs to high-voltage transformers and switchgear because multiple 2026 sources identify electrical equipment shortages as project-timing constraints.
Large-load tariffs are not just policy noise; they are evidence filters that separate speculative megawatt requests from binding customer commitments.
AEP Ohio's binding data-center contract updates and future load-study tranches should be monitored as recurring catalysts for grid-access demand quality.
FERC/PJM co-location rulemaking and related tariff decisions are key catalysts for the nuclear/generation-adjacent data-center model.
Electrical OEM earnings should be tracked for orders, backlog, book-to-bill, capacity additions, transformer lead times, and data-center-specific order growth.
EPC company backlogs and utility transmission awards are the best evidence that tariff-approved load is becoming executable grid capex.
Need more project-level verification linking individual data-center campuses to named transformer, switchgear, substation, and EPC suppliers.
Need market-pricing layer in later funnel stage: many obvious beneficiaries may already reflect strong AI/grid demand in valuation; Layer 2A intentionally excludes valuation judgment.
Need region-by-region mapping for Virginia, Ohio, Texas, Indiana, Illinois, Oregon, Colorado, and Minnesota because tariff rules and grid bottlenecks are state/RTO specific.

summary: Layer 2A industry-chain map for 'New Hotspots': the strongest current interpretation is AI data-center load migrating from a compute-chip story into a power-access, grid-interconnection, electrical-equipment, and thermal-infrastructure bottleneck story. The highest-chokepoint nodes are large-load grid interconnection, utility tariff/cost-allocation rules, high-voltage transformers/switchgear/substations, transmission EPC capacity, firm power procurement, and high-density data-center cooling/power distribution. This is an industry-chain and catalyst map only, not a security recommendation.

supply_chain_map.node: AI compute and hyperscaler data-center demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: GPU clusters and AI workloads create unusually dense, fast-growing power loads; this demand pulls through electricity procurement, interconnection studies, substations, switchgear, transformers, cooling, and EPC capacity.
Data centers may have capital and chips but still cannot energize without utility studies, transmission capacity, network upgrades, signed contracts, collateral, and load certainty.

Tariffs convert speculative load requests into binding commitments and minimum-bill obligations; they also determine whether costs are shifted to general ratepayers or assigned to data-center customers.
New data-center clusters often require upstream transmission upgrades; regulatory treatment of who pays can accelerate, delay, or relocate projects.

Transformers are long-lead, hard-to-substitute electrical assets required both on the grid side and the data-center site side; delays can stop an entire project even if electrical gear is a small percentage of total capex.

supply_chain_map.node: Medium-voltage switchgear, breakers, capacitors, and protection systems
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Switchgear and protection equipment gate safe energization and distribution of multi-megawatt loads; AI buildouts are increasing demand faster than many supply chains can respond.
Substations, HVDC, synchronous condensers, capacitors, and grid-stability equipment become necessary as large loads concentrate in specific regions and stress local transmission systems.

supply_chain_map.node: Transmission, substation, and utility EPC labor
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even when equipment is procured, utilities need qualified engineering, procurement, construction, linemen, and project-management capacity to execute network upgrades.
AI data centers need reliable 24/7 power; nuclear, gas, and structured PPAs can become siting advantages where grid interconnection is constrained.

Generator-adjacent data centers can shorten perceived power-access timelines, but market rules, FERC/PJM policy, transmission charges, and reliability obligations remain unresolved catalysts and risks.
UPS, busway, PDUs, low/medium-voltage distribution, modular power units, and monitoring systems are required to convert grid power into usable rack power.

supply_chain_map.node: Liquid cooling and high-density thermal management
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI rack densities push beyond traditional air-cooling assumptions; direct-to-chip liquid cooling, cold plates, coolant distribution units, and heat rejection systems become gating infrastructure.
Data centers require resilience and ride-through capacity; battery imports and energy-storage components can become secondary supply constraints.

supply_chain_map.node: Utility load forecasting, grid-edge software, metering, and demand response
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As large loads become more volatile and geographically concentrated, utilities need better forecasting, operational visibility, power-quality monitoring, and flexibility tools.
Data-center siting can face pushback over electricity bills, water use, land use, noise, and grid reliability; opposition can slow permits and tariff approvals.
